wine.name: Colomé Altura Máxima Malbec
wine.grapes: Malbec, bottled on its own from the one vineyard.
wine.sites: The Altura Máxima vineyard at Payogasta, in the upper Calchaquí Valleys north of the winery at Molinos, at about 3,111 metres by the house's own figures, on calcareous and granitic soils.
wine.making: Aged in old French oak barrels, of their third and fourth use, for twenty four months by the house's sheets for the 2016, 2017 and 2019 vintages, so the wood frames the fruit rather than flavouring it; the sheets read give no detail of the ferment.
wine.glass: Deep, inky colour; black cherry, plum and violet over black olive, dried herbs and a salty edge, with liquorice on the palate, bright acidity and fine grained, chalky tannin.
wine.ageing: Tight and coiled when young, it opens over five years or so in bottle, and its acidity and firm tannin carry it well beyond a decade.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a large Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Altura Máxima is Bodega Colomé's Malbec from a vineyard at Payogasta that the house puts at about 3,111 metres, high in the Calchaquí Valleys. Inky, salty and violet scented, with chalky tannin, it wants a decanter and red meat.
records.story: Colomé dates itself to 1831, and by its own account it is the oldest winery in Argentina to have made wine without a break since. The house tells that it was founded by a landowner of Molinos who had briefly governed Salta for the Spanish crown in 1809 and 1810, and who fled to his estate at Molinos when the revolution reached the north. The estate lies at about 2,300 metres in the upper Calchaquí Valleys, a long way from the Mendoza vineyards that make most of the country's wine, and the house dates its oldest vines to 1854, when the founder's daughter brought French Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon to the estate. In 2001, by the house's account, a Swiss family bought the estate and the vineyards around it, and planted El Arenal, its first new vineyard, at about 2,600 metres. The Altura Máxima vineyard at Payogasta, further up the valley towards Cachi, came after, at about 3,111 metres; its first years were hard, and the first Altura Máxima Malbec was the 2012 vintage. The wine exists to show what altitude does to Malbec: thick skins and deep colour from the fierce light, acidity from the cold nights. Set beside a Malbec from Luján de Cuyo, it shows how far the grape travels in the north.

wine.sites: A parcel of pergola trained vines planted in 1945, by the house's account, on Finca Las Mercedes in the Cafayate Valley, at about 1,700 metres.
wine.making: Made from the old pergola vines of the one parcel on Finca Las Mercedes as a Torrontés of its own; the house gives six to eight months in the cellar before bottling and names no oak.
wine.glass: Honeysuckle and a Muscat like scent over pineapple, lemon and fresh mint, delicate rather than heady; dry and textured, with zesty acidity and a long, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Made to drink in its first few years, it holds its freshness for about three years by the house's account.

records.table: El Esteco's Old Vines 1945 Torrontés comes from pergola vines planted that year on Finca Las Mercedes in the Cafayate Valley. It smells of honeysuckle and pineapple yet finishes dry and zesty, so pour it cold with spiced food.
records.story: The cellar at Cafayate goes back to 1892, when two French brothers of the Michel family began making wine in the valley, and one of them married into the Torino family. From that marriage came the name Michel Torino, under which the house was known for most of the twentieth century and which survives as one range of its wines. Its vineyards lie at about 1,700 metres around the town, and some were planted in the middle of the century on the high pergolas, the parral, that shade the bunches from the hard sun. One parcel on Finca Las Mercedes was planted in 1945, and the house later made its fruit into a wine of its own. The family sold the house in the 1990s or about the turn of the century, the accounts differing, and in 2004 the Peñaflor group bought it and gave it the name El Esteco. Under that name it built a range called Old Vines, each wine from an estate more than fifty years old and named for its planting year. The 1945 Torrontés is the white of that range, and it shows what old vines add to the grape: texture and restraint over perfume alone.

wine.name: Etchart Arnaldo B. Gran Reserva
wine.grapes: Malbec, about three fifths, with Cabernet Sauvignon and smaller parts of Tannat and, in some vintages, Petit Verdot; the blend moves from year to year.
wine.sites: The house's vineyards in the Cafayate Valley, around its old estate of La Florida, at about 1,750 metres by its sheet for the 2020 vintage.
wine.making: Aged in oak barrels before bottling: French and American wood for fifteen months by the house's English sheet, and first use French oak by its sheet for the 2020 vintage; the sheets read give no detail of the ferment.
wine.glass: Cassis and blackcurrant over cedar, toasted wood and vanilla, with violet, clove and olive; full bodied, with abundant, dusty tannin and a dry finish.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink a few years after release, it keeps for some ten years in a good vintage, its tannin softening as the fruit dries.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Bodegas Etchart named its red for the man who bought the Cafayate winery in 1938 and first released it in 1990 as Arnaldo B. Mostly Malbec with Cabernet Sauvignon and Tannat, aged in oak, it is dense and dusty, so decant it beside grilled beef.
records.story: By the house's account, wine was first made at La Florida, just outside Cafayate, in 1850, when a local landowner planted vines in what was then a remote corner of the north. In 1938, by the house's account, the winery was bought by a man who had married into the founding family, and it has carried his surname, Etchart, ever since; the house dates the growth of the valley's wine from that purchase. The family then built the Etchart name into a brand known well beyond the valley. In 1990 the house launched Arnaldo B., a red blend named in his honour and the wine it calls its icon, born of its trials of European red grapes in the valley. In the middle of the 1990s the family sold Bodegas Etchart to the Pernod Ricard group, the sources differing between 1995 and 1996, and the family went on to make wine at San Pedro de Yacochuya in the hills above the town. Arnaldo B. has stayed the house's red at the head of its range, Malbec led, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Tannat, the valley's two other firm reds. For a student it ties two Cafayate houses to one family, and shows how the valley's reds turned towards ageing.

wine.name: Yacochuya Malbec
wine.grapes: Malbec, all or nearly all of it, from old vines; some accounts give a small share of Cabernet Sauvignon in some vintages.
wine.sites: Old Malbec vines on a steep slope at about 2,000 metres, north west of Cafayate, watered by furrows from mountain springs; the vines are more than sixty years old by two accounts, and older by others.
wine.making: The old vine Malbec is fermented and then aged for about eighteen months in French oak barriques, all or most of them new by the accounts read for several vintages, so the oak shows clearly in a young bottle.
wine.glass: Blackberry, plum and fig over chocolate, black olive and lavender; massive, ripe and high in alcohol, with thick tannin, and with age a bouquet of prune and tobacco.
wine.ageing: Dense and closed for its first years, it is built for the cellar, and older vintages have shown a mature bouquet after a decade and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours; a large Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Yacochuya is a dense Malbec from old vines on a slope at about 2,000 metres above Cafayate, made by the Etchart family with a Bordeaux consultant. Ripe, massive and oaky when young, it needs years in bottle and a decanter.
records.story: The Etchart family had made wine in Cafayate since 1938, when the father bought the winery at La Florida, and in 1987 or 1988, the accounts differing, the family brought a Bordeaux consultant to the valley. The consultant, the story goes, was taken with an old Malbec vineyard on the steep slopes of Yacochuya, high above the town, and the two men set out to make a Malbec there for the cellar rather than for the table. In the middle of the 1990s the family sold Bodegas Etchart, and the family turned to the new estate. Building of the winery on the hillside began in 1998, and it received its first vintage in February 1999, by two accounts. The vines, at about 2,000 metres, are old Malbec, fed by spring water carried in furrows. Yacochuya is the estate's Malbec from those vines, aged in French oak; the San Pedro de Yacochuya red, a Malbec with some Cabernet Sauvignon, is its second wine. For a student it stands for a turn in Argentine wine, towards dense reds made to age, and for the reach of Bordeaux consultants into the high north.

wine.name: Laborum Single Vineyard Torrontés, Finca El Retiro
wine.sites: Finca El Retiro, by the house's account its oldest vineyard, in the town of Cafayate at about 1,650 metres: old vines on pergolas in sandy soil that holds their vigour down and keeps the yield low.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented with selected yeasts in concrete eggs, then kept on its lees in the same eggs for about eight months, by the house's sheet; an oak fermented Laborum Torrontés is made apart.
wine.glass: Lychee, passion fruit and grape blossom over grapefruit and orange peel, with a light note of white pepper; more delicate than many Torrontés, dry, with fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: At its freshest in its first few years for its scent, though the lees and the old vines give it texture enough to hold a little longer.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass with room for the scent.

records.table: El Porvenir de Cafayate makes its Laborum Torrontés from Finca El Retiro, an old pergola vineyard in the town itself, fermented and kept on its lees in concrete eggs. Lychee and grape blossom, then a dry, fresh finish: pour it cold with ceviche.
records.story: El Porvenir de Cafayate is a young house in an old setting. Its cellar is an old adobe building in the centre of Cafayate, and one guide holds that the bodega was first built by Italian immigrants early in the twentieth century. The family behind the house had come to wine in the valley at Tolombón, where it bought an old winery making bulk wine in the late 1970s or the 1980s by different accounts. In 2000, by two guides, the family bought El Porvenir and set about modernising it, with Finca El Retiro among its vineyards. That vineyard, in the town itself, is the house's oldest: its Torrontés stands on pergolas in sandy soil, planted in 1945 by one of the house's sheets and in 1950 by its vineyard page. The house built its range in tiers, with Amauta for blends, Laborum for single vineyard wines of one variety, and Porvenir for the blend at the head of the range, and in the Laborum range it bottles Torrontés from El Retiro, a red of Tannat and others besides. The El Retiro Torrontés is the white abroad that carries the house's name. For a student it shows the valley's grape from old pergola vines, made with lees and concrete rather than perfume alone.

others.name: Laborum Tannat
others.note: A single vineyard Tannat of the Laborum range, the valley's firm red grape.

traps: Laborum is a range of single vineyard wines, not one wine: there is a Torrontés, an oak fermented Torrontés and reds under the name.
Porvenir is the blend that heads the house's range; Laborum sits beneath it and holds the single vineyard wines.

cards.front: El Porvenir de Cafayate: what vineyard gives its Laborum Torrontés?
cards.back: Finca El Retiro, by the house's account its oldest vineyard, on pergolas in the town of Cafayate.

cards.front: In what vessel does the Laborum Single Vineyard Torrontés rest on its lees?
cards.back: Concrete eggs, for about eight months, by the house's sheet.

questions.q: How are the old Torrontés vines of El Porvenir's Finca El Retiro trained?
opts: On high pergolas
As free standing bush vines
On low wires close to the ground
Up chestnut stakes on terraces
questions.exp: Finca El Retiro is a pergola vineyard, the parral of the valley, which shades the bunches; bush vines are the old form of other regions, not of this site.

questions.q: In which year, by two guides, did the family behind El Porvenir de Cafayate buy the house?
questions.exp: The family bought El Porvenir in 2000 and modernised it; 1892 is the start of El Esteco's cellar and 1938 the Etchart purchase.

report: The pick in doubt is confirmed: Laborum is the house's single vineyard, single variety range, so the record teaches its Torrontés from Finca El Retiro; the house's top blend is Porvenir, which a checker may prefer as the flagship, though the El Retiro Torrontés is the wine critics and importers abroad meet most.

Founded is empty: the family bought the house in 2000 by Fodor's and Cream Wine, but the cellar is older, built by Italian immigrants early in the twentieth century by Fodor's alone, which the story hedges.
The family's start at Tolombón is the late 1970s by Cream Wine and the 1980s by La Gaceta, so both are given; the family is living and not named, nor its former governor.
El Retiro's planting year is 1945 on the product sheet and 1950 on the vineyard page, both the house's, and the story gives both.
Concrete eggs and eight months on lees come from the house's sheet for the de Parcela bottling; older Single Vineyard vintages may have been made otherwise.
The region's producers line speaks of Malbec and Tannat from sandy soils; the sources read confirm Tannat and Malbec in the range but not their soils.

open: The flagship stays the Laborum Torrontés of Finca El Retiro; the integrator may weigh the Porvenir blend, which heads the range, though the El Retiro Torrontés is the wine met abroad.
